In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
radix sort is the fastest for small data sizes and keys and merge sort is the fastest when the keys are large and data sizes are large.
radix sort is better on current CPUs, but merge sort is better on future CPUs and on current GPUs.
merge sort is better for large key sizes and large SIMD widths.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the performance of sorting algorithms depends on the architecture, and that the best sorting algorithm depends on the key size and the architecture.
the performance gap between radix sort and merge sort is narrowing, and that merge sort will be the winner on large key sizes in the future.
radix sort is a better choice for current architectures and merge sort is better for future architectures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice between comparison and non-comparative sort algorithms should be based on the size of the key rather than the data size.
future database architectures should be designed for high bandwidth utilization and large SIMD width.
the best performing sorting algorithm on a given architecture is not necessarily the best performing sorting implementation on a future architecture.
